scenes.text: Your brain tends to like things simply because it has seen them before.
Psychologists call this the mere exposure effect.
In the nineteen sixties, psychologist Robert Zajonc tested it in a series of experiments.
He showed people nonsense words, drawings, photos of faces and unfamiliar symbols.
The things people had seen more often were rated more positively.
Later studies flashed images so fast that people could not recognize them.
Yet people still tended to prefer the ones they had been shown.
There's even a strange classroom story from Oregon State University.
A student came to class inside a big black bag, with only his feet showing.
At first his classmates were hostile, then curious, and finally friendly.
A review of two hundred and eight experiments found the effect is reliable.
But it has limits, because after too many repeats, liking can drop again.
That's how a catchy song can go from great to annoying.
What song did you love at first, then get sick of?

title: Why you like things you've seen before 👀
caption: It's called the mere exposure effect: seeing something again and again tends to make us like it more. But too much repetition can flip it.
